title: Savitri and Satyavan
hook: Narada praises the young man Savitri has chosen, then names his one flaw: he will die within a year
carry: say aloud what you've already decided

segments.voice: Yesterday began the story of Savitri and Satyavan: a princess sent out to choose, who came home with the name of an exiled king's son. Your line was make one choice fully your own. What choice did you stand behind? Day seven hundred ninety-six.

Savitri has just said his name, and the sage Narada says: oh no. He doesn't mean the young man is bad. Quite the opposite. Ashvapati asks him what's wrong with Satyavan, and Narada starts listing what's right. He's truthful. He's generous. He's patient, handsome, kind to everyone. Every good thing you could want. And then the sage stops, and says there's one flaw, and it outweighs all the rest. Here is the hinge of the whole story, said aloud at a royal court.
screen: `NARADA SAYS: OH NO.` → `EVERYTHING RIGHT ABOUT HIM.` → `AND ONE FLAW.`

segments.voice: The flaw is this, Narada says: a year from today, Satyavan will die. The court goes quiet. Her father turns to Savitri at once. Go, he says, choose someone else. And Savitri's answer is the center of today. In the telling, she says something like this: some things happen only once. A daughter is given in marriage once. A person says I give, once. I have chosen once. Whether his life is long or short, whether he is full of virtues or not, I have chosen my husband, and I won't choose twice. My mind decided first, then my words said it, and now I'll act on it. Look at the shape of what she says. She doesn't argue that Narada is wrong. She doesn't promise to fix it. She hears terrible news and keeps her word anyway, because to her, a choice of the heart is a promise already made. And Narada, the one who brought the bad news, doesn't argue with her. He tells the king: her mind is steady. Let it be. Then he blesses the marriage and goes. So Ashvapati travels into the forest to find old blind Dyumatsena under a tree. The exiled king is worried. We have lost our kingdom, he says. We live on what the forest gives. How could a princess bear this life? Ashvapati answers that his daughter already knows all of it. The two fathers agree. And Savitri is married to Satyavan, there among the hermitages, carrying a piece of news her husband doesn't know.
screen: `"A YEAR FROM TODAY."` · `"CHOOSE SOMEONE ELSE."` · `"I HAVE CHOSEN ONCE."` · then, large: `MARRIED IN THE FOREST, KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle by itself. Savitri said: first the mind decided, then the words, then the acts. Bring to mind one thing you've already decided in your own mind but haven't yet said aloud. Breathe in, and hold the decision as it is. Breathe out, and imagine saying it, plainly, to the person it concerns. You don't have to act on it today. Just notice the step between deciding and saying. If you pray, you can bring that decision into your prayer. If not, simply rest with it, quietly. The bell holds the time.
Satyavan. The truthful, generous son with one year left to live, chosen anyway by a bride who says she has chosen once, and won't choose twice.
Your line: say aloud what you've already decided. Today, say aloud one thing you've already decided, so the word can follow the mind. Day seven hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: In the Mahabharata's telling, Narada's warning and Savitri's reply that she chooses only once both come before the wedding, so she marries Satyavan already knowing about the year.

pairs: asks if a princess can bear the forest

options: say you have chosen once, and won't choose twice.
ask the sage to change his words.
fork.reveal: she keeps her choice, Narada tells the king her mind is steady, and the marriage goes ahead in the forest.

original.note: Sanskrit Satyavan, the son of Dyumatsena whom Narada praises as truthful.

trapdoor: what you thought: Savitri didn't know what she was getting into.
what it means: she heard the warning and kept her choice, saying a choice is made only once.
what a scholar hears: the warning comes before the wedding, so the story never asks whether she knew, only what she will do with the year.

notes: All paraphrase. The 'a year' span is stated in the text (Narada's warning); confirm it is within the claims rule.
Savitri's reply ('once ... once ... once'; mind, then words, then acts) is paraphrased, not quoted; confirm against Ganguli.
Narada's opening reaction is rendered informally ('oh no'); confirm the text has him express dismay before listing Satyavan's virtues.
The text explains Satyavan's name by his parents' truthfulness; not taught here to avoid an etymology claim, though the original note says Narada praises him as truthful.
Day 797 (written separately) opens with Savitri in the hermitage, jewels set aside; this day stops at the marriage to avoid repeating it.
